The river learned patience from the stones it carried.
It did not rush to be useful. It moved around edges, over bark, through moss, and let the world rearrange itself in its wake. Every stone wore a smile, polished by years of gentle conversation. The water never needed a destination; the destination followed.

I used to think freedom meant running. I chased it through open fields, through crowded stations, through the bright glass of a future that kept changing its clothes. But one morning the rain tapped a slow rhythm on the window and I remembered that there are freedoms smaller than oceans. A cup warmed in both hands. A sentence unfinished, then finished. A door left open only enough.

The city hummed with its thousand small urgences. A bus exhaled, a stranger laughed, bread cooled in a paper bag. I stood among them and felt less like a passenger and more like a witness. To witness is not passive. It gathers attention the way a stone gathers rain.

Perhaps I am tired of speed. Perhaps I want to be slowed into meaning. I want to sit where the streetlight bends and watch the sky decide. I want to let my feet find the path instead of my mind dictating it. If the river can make a place out of moving, maybe I can make a life out of paying attention, one quiet, willing breath at a time. Soft light returned, patient and warm, as if waiting for something known.
